newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. chief faces test in revamping Rwanda tribunal.
newsitem.headline: U.N. chief faces test in revamping Rwanda tribunal.

text.p: After a scathing report of mismanagement in the U.N. Rwanda genocide tribunal, Secretary-General Kofi Annan has to decide quickly what changes to make to restore confidence in the trials.

"We owe it to the half million victims of genocide in Rwanda to do better than we have done," said U.N. spokesman Fred Eckhard on Wednesday. Annan, he said, was "struck by the breath of the criticism."

The report by Karl Paschke, a German diplomat who heads the U.N. Office of Internal Oversight Services, said the court was riddled with mismanagement, waste, unqualified personnel and bureaucratic infighting.
"Not a single administrative area," he said, "functioned effectively."

Created by the U.N. Security Council more than two years ago, the tribunal is to try leaders responsible for more than half a million Tutsis and moderate Hutus massacred in Rwanda in 1994 by Hutu troops and others.
The court has indicted 21 people and is currently conducting its first trial in Arusha, Tanzania. A sub-office for prosecutors and investigators is in Kigali, Rwanda.

Annan has called three senior officials to New York on Feb. 21 and will decide on further action at that time. They include Prosecutor Louise Arbor of Canada, Deputy Prosecutor Honoure Rakotomanana of Madagascar and Registrar Andronico Adede of Kenya.
Arbor is also chief prosecutor for the U.N. tribunal on war crimes in the former Yugoslavia and is based in the Hague.

U.N. sources said she would probably not renew the contract of Rakotomanana when it expired in March. Paschke in the report criticised his Kigali office for bad management and ignoring instructions on legal strategy.

Paschke's report, which followed a two-month investigation of the court, was most harsh on abuses in the registrar's department. Adede himself was cited for spending nearly half his time on official travel.

But he told reporters he was not recommending Adede be dismissed because of the many complex tasks he managed to carry out in setting up a new centre with hardly any support or proper backup from New York headquarters.
U.N. sources, however, said Annan had not reached a decision yet on Adede's future.
The controversy surrounding the court surfaced several months ago with various employees accusing tribunal officials of nepotism in hiring relatives, friends or lovers.

But Paschke, in answer to questions, said he was unable to substantiate these allegations. He also avoided accusations of financial corruption, saying that the mismangement of funds were not necessarily intentional.

Since the charges surfaced, key administrators in Arusha have been replaced and the New York departments of human resources and administration and management have intervened to recruit staff and evaluate those on the scene.
Both departments, along with legal affairs, were sharply criticised by Paschke for abdicating their responsibilities and neglecting the tribunal, particularly in its early stages.
